metadata.site: Gale Crater / Mount Sharp, Mars — 6 km study area centered 5.10°S, 137.75°E
metadata.selectionNote: Our selection based on published Curiosity mission traverse data and science reports. Coordinates are representative positions inside the 6 km planning area; the named geological units are real features studied by Curiosity nearby. Labeled 'our selection' throughout the app.
metadata.coordinateSystem: IAU2000 areocentric latitude, east positive longitude

properties.name: Murray Buttes Boxwork
properties.why: Eroded boxwork ridges in sulfate/mudstone layers — the primary science goal of this Marswalk.
properties.detail: Curiosity documented boxwork formations at Murray Buttes: erosion-resistant veins form ridge networks as surrounding mudstone weathers away. These record the chemistry of ancient groundwater that likely supported a habitable environment. Rapin et al. (2021) identified similar sulfate-bearing boxwork ridges as evidence of cyclical wet/dry periods.
properties.findings: Sulfate-rich veins (calcium sulfate / gypsum), dark mudstone matrix, erosion-resistant ridge networks. Sample targets: fresh vein cross-sections for groundwater chemistry; mudstone flakes for organic compound analysis. Look for color contrasts between pale veins and dark host rock.
properties.selectionNote: Our selection — representative position inside study area

properties.name: Glen Torridon Clay Unit
properties.why: Strongest evidence of a long-lived ancient lake. Clay minerals form only when water persists for thousands of years.
properties.detail: Glen Torridon hosts the largest clay mineral deposits found by Curiosity. Bristow et al. (2021) showed iron-magnesium smectite clays require prolonged water contact to form — strong evidence the ancient lake in Gale Crater persisted for geologically significant time. A human geologist could sample fresh outcrop faces inaccessible to the rover arm.
properties.findings: Iron-magnesium smectite clays (grey-green outcrops), fine-grained mudstone layers, possible organic-rich laminations. Sample targets: fresh outcrop faces not weathered by UV; clay-rich nodules; bedding contacts between clay and sulfate layers. The grey-green color distinguishes clay from surrounding reddish terrain.
properties.source: Bristow et al. (2021), Science Advances, doi:10.1126/sciadv.abh3023
properties.selectionNote: Our selection — representative position inside study area

properties.name: Vera Rubin Ridge
properties.why: Hematite-rich layer formed in ancient standing water. The ridge is a natural waypoint and navigation landmark.
properties.detail: Vera Rubin Ridge is an iron-oxide (hematite) bearing unit that forms a prominent east-west ridge. Fraeman et al. (2020) showed the hematite formed in acidic to neutral standing water. Its hardness made it resistant to erosion, creating a natural path along the ridge with panoramic views of the crater floor below.
properties.findings: Grey hematite (iron oxide) nodules and coatings, iron-enriched bedrock layers, possible jarosite (iron sulfate). The reddish-grey rock has a dull metallic luster. Sample targets: hematite-coated pebbles; bedrock at the ridge crest showing iron enrichment banding; contact zone where hematite layer meets underlying mudstone.
properties.source: Fraeman et al. (2020), JGR Planets, doi:10.1029/2019JE006306

properties.name: Gediz Vallis Channel
properties.why: Possible water-carved channel on the flank of Mount Sharp. Could reveal the most recent wet period on Mars.
properties.detail: Gediz Vallis is an erosional channel cutting through the sulfate unit of Mount Sharp. NASA (2023) reported that Curiosity found evidence the channel was carved by liquid water relatively recently in Mars history, potentially billions of years after the ancient lake dried up. A human explorer could investigate channel walls and floor deposits unreachable by the rover.
properties.findings: Rounded pebbles and cobbles (transported by water), layered sulfate deposits on channel walls, possible salt crusts at the base. Sample targets: rounded vs. angular clasts to confirm water transport; fine-grained lag deposit on the channel floor; fresh cross-sections of the channel wall stratigraphy. Rounded rocks = water-tumbled evidence.
properties.source: NASA/JPL press release, 2023; MSL Science Team
properties.selectionNote: Our selection — representative position inside study area

properties.name: Greenheugh Pediment
properties.why: Erosion-resistant sandstone cap preserving a climate transition layer — evidence of a drier Mars era following the ancient lake.
properties.detail: Greenheugh Pediment is a broad, gently-sloping erosional surface capped by coarse sandstone. Edgar et al. (2020) showed it records a major climate transition: sandstone deposited by wind (aeolian) overlies older lake-deposited mudstone, marking the moment the persistent lake dried. A human explorer at this boundary could collect samples at the contact zone.
properties.findings: Coarse cross-bedded sandstone (wind-deposited), sharp contact with underlying fine mudstone, possible lag boulders armoring the pediment surface. Sample targets: the exact mudstone-to-sandstone contact layer (the climate transition); coarse grains for aeolian grain-size analysis; any cementation minerals at the contact. The contact is visually distinct: rough coarse cap over smooth fine layers.
properties.source: Edgar et al. (2020), JGR Planets, doi:10.1029/2020JE006527
